title: Towards Token-Level Text Anomaly Detection
summary: Existing text anomaly detection methods only work at the document level (or on narrow, task-specific token tasks such as spell checking), so they cannot localize which tokens in a text are anomalous. The paper introduces token-level text anomaly detection, releases three token-annotated benchmarks (SMS_Spam with injected character corruption, Restaurant Review semantic anomalies, Grammar errors), and proposes TokenCore, which builds a memory bank of normal word-level token embeddings (BERT-base-uncased embeddings aggregated by element-wise max pooling over subwords) and scores each test token by its nearest-neighbor distance, aggregating token scores by mean for document-level scores. TokenCore achieves the best average token-level AUROC (0.7145) and document-level AUROC (0.7335) among 7 methods, ranking first at token level on Review (0.8271) and Grammar (0.6371) and at document level on Review (0.9594), while ECOD/iForest remain better on the character-corruption SMS_Spam token-level task.

target.split: Test = 50% of documents not used as normal training data (normal + anomalous); token-level scoring over test documents

why: The authors released the method code (TokenCore.py: memory bank + nearest-neighbor token scoring), the alignment/annotation utilities (align.py, tokens_labels/json_to_npy.py) and all three annotated datasets locally in data/ (grammar .npy/.json, restaurant_review, sms_spam), so the core logic can be kept verbatim. What is NOT released is a runnable entrypoint: the only end-to-end artifact is Demo.ipynb (with frozen outputs), there is no requirements.txt, and TokenCore.py consumes precomputed token-embedding matrices, so the BERT-base-uncased embedding extraction, the 50/50 split and the token-level AUROC computation have to be rebuilt as a script from the notebook before the target number for Grammar (C1) can be produced. Keep authors' logic, rebuild the missing driver.
est_runtime: ~25-35 min wall clock on 22 CPU cores / 15.4 GB RAM: ~10 min installing torch (CPU wheel), transformers, scikit-learn; ~1 min BERT-base download; ~1-3 min BERT forward pass over 300 short Grammar documents; seconds for the max-pooling, memory-bank build and brute-force nearest-neighbor scoring; plus the driver-script rewrite from the notebook and one clean end-to-end re-run.
blockers: no dependency file: torch/transformers/sklearn/numpy must be pinned by hand (works on Python 3.12)
TokenCore.py takes embedding matrices only; the BERT max-pooling-over-subwords front-end exists only inside the notebook, so the pipeline must be extracted into a script
Demo.ipynb is 3.8 MB of stored outputs; it must be rewritten/cleared before execution
no GPU on this machine (BERT-base CPU inference only, which is acceptable at this scale)

Grammar token-level AUROC is computed over very few anomalous tokens (~15 anomalous docs in the test half), and the split is random, so the absolute value 0.6371 will depend on the split seed and may drift

approach: This is a partial_release reproduction of claim C1: TokenCore's token-level AUROC on the Grammar benchmark (0.6371, tolerance ±0.02 absolute). We clone the authors' repo, keep TokenCore.py/align.py/json_to_npy.py verbatim, and rebuild only the missing driver that Demo.ipynb used to hide: read the released grammar annotations (data/grammar_correction_labeled.json and data/grammar.npy), build the 300-document corpus (270 normal / 30 anomalous, R10), take 50% of the normal documents as the memory-bank training set (R6, A8), run BERT-base-uncased over the remaining normal + anomalous documents, max-pool subword embeddings into word units aligned with the gold word-level token labels (Eq. 1, R2/R9, A3/A4), fit the authors' TextCore memory bank on normal-training token embeddings only (R3, A2), score every test token by Euclidean nearest-neighbour distance (Eq. 2, R4, A1/A9), and compute pooled token-level AUROC/AUPRC plus the mean-aggregated document-level scores (Eq. 3, R5, A5). The paper value is a single split-free number, so the only real drift risk is split randomness on 300 short documents; we therefore report a primary seeded run plus a small multi-seed spread so the ±0.02 band can be interpreted. Only the Grammar dataset is needed for C1, but the same driver is written so that running it on restaurant_review / sms_spam later costs nothing extra.
steps: Clone https://github.com/charles-cao/TokenCore.git into ./TokenCore and record the commit hash; do not modify TokenCore.py, align.py or tokens_labels/json_to_npy.py.

Create a venv/conda env on Python 3.12 and pip install torch (CPU wheel from the default index), transformers, numpy, scikit-learn, tqdm, requests; write the resolved versions into requirements.txt (the file the README references but the repo lacks).

Run src/inspect_data.py: dump shapes/dtypes/keys of data/grammar.npy and the JSON schema of data/grammar_correction_labeled.json, and print the actual class/function signatures of TokenCore.py and align.py. Decide the exact field names for words, token labels and document labels, and confirm the .npy is a token/label array rather than precomputed embeddings (43 KB is far too small for 300x768 floats).

Implement src/data_grammar.py against the inspected schema; load all 300 Grammar documents and hard-assert 300 documents / 270 normal / 30 anomalous (10% rate, R10) and consistency of the document labels with the token labels (R11).

Implement the split: with seed 0, shuffle the 270 normal documents, take the first 135 as the memory-bank training set; the test set is the other 135 normal documents plus all 30 anomalous documents (165 docs). Export the token-level gold labels for every test token.

Implement src/embed_bert.py: tokenize with BertTokenizerFast(return_offsets_mapping / word_ids), run BertModel in eval() with torch.no_grad() in batches of 32, max_length 128, take last_hidden_state, drop special tokens, and element-wise max-pool subwords per word unit. Assert a 1:1 map between produced word units and the gold word tokens in the annotated JSON; if align.py exposes an alignment helper, call it instead of re-implementing.

Implement src/detector.py: import the authors' TokenCore (use the real class name found by inspect_data.py, README shows both TokenCore and TextCore) and its fit / decision_function, fit on the normal-training token embedding matrix (no anomalous tokens, R3) and score the test token embeddings (R4).

Implement src/evaluate.py: token-level AUROC/AUPRC pooled over all test tokens (micro), document-level scores as the per-document mean of token scores (R5) and their AUROC/AUPRC, plus a random-score control (expected AUROC ~0.5) to validate the metric plumbing.
Wire reproduce.py to run the whole chain end-to-end; run the smoke configuration first (see smoke_test) and confirm all assertions on counts and shapes pass.
Run the intermediate checks (see intermediate_checks) before the full run.

Full run: python reproduce.py --datasets grammar --seed 0 (CPU-only BERT inference over 300 short sentences, seconds for the memory bank and brute-force L2 nearest-neighbour search). Write results/metrics.json.

If |token_auroc_grammar - 0.6371| > 0.02, re-run with seeds 1 and 2 and inspect sensitivity: report the per-seed values and mean/std, and check the highest-risk choices first (A5 micro vs per-document AUROC, A1/A9 Euclidean on unnormalized embeddings, A4 whether punctuation units are scored).
Write the final results/metrics.json containing the primary value, the multi-seed spread, the target, the tolerance band and an explicit pass/fail flag.
smoke_test: python reproduce.py --datasets grammar --smoke --seed 0 -> loads the released grammar annotations, keeps only the first 8 normal + first 2 anomalous documents (forcing the split so both sides are non-empty), runs one BERT-base forward pass over those 10 documents, max-pools subwords, builds a ~100-200 entry memory bank, scores the test tokens, and prints token_auroc/token_auprc plus every shape (n_docs, n_word_units, n_bank_tokens, n_test_tokens, n_positive_tokens). Success = no exception, finite scores, 1:1 alignment between word units and gold tokens, and AUROC in [0,1]. This exercises every stage of the data flow in under a minute.
intermediate_checks: Dataset size and label rate: exactly 300 documents, 270 normal (token_labels all 0) and 30 anomalous (>=1 token_label = 1) = 10% anomaly rate (R10); stop if the released file deviates.
Document/token label consistency: every document with at least one 1 token has doc_label 1 and vice versa (R11).

Token-level class balance: report total tokens, total anomalous tokens and their fraction across all 300 docs, and across the 165 test docs; sanity expectation is a few percent (the contract quotes token AUPRC ~0.04 for Grammar, which is roughly the positive rate) and only a handful of positives, so AUROC variance across seeds will be large - this justifies the ±0.02 band.
Alignment coverage: fraction of gold word tokens that receive a BERT word unit (target 1.0); log any word that tokenizes to zero subwords or overflows max_length=128.
Split sizes: 135 normal training docs and 135 normal + 30 anomalous test docs with seed 0; training set contains zero anomalous tokens (R3).

Memory bank size: n_bank_tokens should equal the total number of word units in the 135 normal training documents (report it; expect a few thousand) - a much smaller number means documents were dropped silently.

Parameter/embedding check: assert the token embedding width is 768 and that the pooling really is element-wise max (a max-pooled vector must equal the coordinate-wise max of its subword vectors on a hand-checked example).

Sanity baseline: random token scores give AUROC ~0.5 and AUPRC ~positive rate; TokenCore scores on the training tokens themselves (excluding self-matches) give near-zero distances, confirming the nearest-neighbour direction (higher distance = more anomalous, R4).
Metric parity: verify the AUROC/AUPRC implementation against sklearn.roc_auc_score / average_precision_score on synthetic labels, so the 0.6371 comparison cannot fail for plumbing reasons.
budget_plan: Total ~30-35 min on 22 CPU cores / 15.4 GB RAM. Setup 10 min: clone the repo (<1 min) and pip install the CPU torch wheel plus transformers/scikit-learn (~8-9 min, ~5 GB, the dominant cost). Reconnaissance 3 min: inspect_data.py plus reading TokenCore.py/align.py and the JSON schema. Implementation 8 min: data_grammar.py, embed_bert.py, detector.py, evaluate.py, reproduce.py, requirements.txt. Smoke 2 min: 10-document subset end-to-end. Intermediate checks 2 min: counts, rates, alignment coverage, bank size, metric parity. Full run 3-4 min: one BERT-base forward pass over 300 short Grammar sentences on CPU (1-3 min) plus seconds of max-pooling and brute-force L2 nearest-neighbour scoring. Verification 3 min: compare against 0.6371 with the ±0.02 band, and if out of band spend up to 5 more minutes on seeds 1 and 2 and on the highest-risk assumptions (A5, A1/A9, A4). Keep ~3 min slack; only the Grammar dataset is run, so no SMS_Spam/Review time is spent.

    9|         """
   10|         Parameters
   11|         ----------
   12|         n_neighbors : int, default=1
   13|             Number of neighbors to use
   14|         aggregation : str, default='mean'
   15|             How to aggregate distances when n_neighbors > 1
   16|             Options: 'mean', 'max', 'min', 'median'
   17|         """
   18|         self.n_neighbors = n_neighbors
   19|         self.aggregation = aggregation
   20|         self.nbrs = None
   21|         
   22|     def fit(self, X):
   23|         """
   24|         Fit the model using X as training data
   25|         
   26|         Parameters
   27|         ----------
   28|         X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
   29|             Training data
   30|             
   31|         Returns
   32|         -------
   33|         self : object
   34|             Fitted estimator
   35|         """
   36|         self.nbrs = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=self.n_neighbors).fit(X)
   37|         return self
   38|     
   39|     def decision_function(self, X):
   40|         """
   41|         Compute anomaly scores for samples in X
   42|         
   43|         Parameters
   44|         ----------
   45|         X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
   46|             Test data
   47|             
   48|         Returns
   49|         -------
   50|         scores : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
   51|             Anomaly scores (higher means more anomalous)
   52|         """
   53|         distances, _ = self.nbrs.kneighbors(X)
   54|         
   55|         # If n_neighbors == 1, distances is (n_samples, 1), just flatten
   56|         if self.n_neighbors == 1:
   57|             scores = distances.flatten()
   58|         else:
   59|             # Aggregate multiple neighbor distances
   60|             if self.aggregation == 'mean':
   61|                 scores = np.mean(distances, axis=1)
   62|             elif self.aggregation == 'max':
   63|                 scores = np.max(distances, axis=1)
   64|             elif self.aggregation == 'min':

    1| # TokenCore
    2| 
    3| Official code and datasets for the paper
    4| **[Towards Token-Level Text Anomaly Detection](https://huggingface.co/papers/2601.13644)** (WWW '26).
    5| 
    6| TokenCore is a memory-bank method for **token-level text anomaly detection**: instead of only flagging whole documents as anomalous, it localizes *which specific tokens* are anomalous. It builds a memory bank of normal token embeddings and scores each test token by its distance to the nearest normal neighbor, then aggregates token scores to obtain document-level scores.
    7| 
    8| ## Datasets
    9| 
   10| The three benchmark datasets are hosted on the Hugging Face Hub:
   11| 
   12| 👉 **[https://huggingface.co/datasets/Charles-Cao/TokenAD](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Charles-Cao/TokenAD)**
   13| 
   14| Each dataset provides both document-level and token-level anomaly annotations.
   15| 
   16| | Dataset | Anomaly type | Documents | Anomalies | Rate |
   17| |---|---|---|---|---|
   18| | SMS Spam | Character-level (corrupted sequences) | 4,518 | 393 | 8.7% |
   19| | Restaurant Review | Semantic (negative sentiment) | 1,100 | 50 | 4.5% |
   20| | Grammar Correction | Grammatical errors | 300 | 30 | 10% |
   21| 
   22| A local copy is also available in the `data/` folder.
   23| 
   24| ## Installation
   25| 
   26| ```bash
   27| git clone https://github.com/charles-cao/TokenCore.git
   28| cd TokenCore
   29| pip install -r requirements.txt
   30| ```
   31| 
   32| ## Quick Start
   33| 
   34| ```python
   35| from TokenCore import TextCore
   36| 
   37| model = TokenCore()
   38| 
   39| # Fit on normal token embeddings
   40| model.fit(X_train)
   41| 
   42| # Get token-level anomaly scores
   43| scores = model.decision_function(X_test)
   44| ```
   45| 
   46| `X_train` and `X_test` are token embedding matrices (e.g. BERT embeddings with max-pooling over subwords). See `Demo.ipynb` for the full pipeline, including embedding extraction, token-level scoring, and document-level aggregation.

! I've recovered the authors' exact `split_anomaly_data`:

```python
def split_anomaly_data(X, y, z, train_ratio=0.5, random_state=42):
    y = np.array(y)
    n_train = int(len

(X) * train_ratio)
    normal_indices = np.where(y == 0)[0]
    np.random.seed(random_state)
    train_indices = np.random.choice(normal_indices, n_train, replace=False)   # kwargs size, replace -> actually CALL_FUNCTION_KW with

('size','replace')? 
    test_indices = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X)), train_indices)
    X_train = [X[i] for i in train_indices]
    y_train = y[train_indices]
    X_test = [X[i] for i

in test_indices]
    y_test = y[test_indices]
    z_train = [z[i] for i in train_indices]
    z_test = [z[i] for i in test_indices]
    return X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, z_train, z_test
```

Wait: CALL_FUNCTION_KW(3 total) with const tuple ('size','replace') and args: normal_indices, n_train, False. Hmm, that means the call is `np.random.choice(normal_indices, size=n_train, replace=False)`. Yes!

The second positional is n_train but passed as keyword `size`. Same result.

Important: `n_train = int(len(X) * train_ratio)` = int(300*0.5) = 150 — that's
50% of ALL documents, drawn from the normal indices only! So training set = 150 normal docs (out of 270), test = 120 normal + 30 anomalous = 150 docs. That matches "We use 50% normal documents

as training data, the rest of data are set as testing" — well, 50% of total documents chosen among normals. Hmm, the paper says "50% normal documents as training data". The authors' code uses int(len(X)*
train_ratio) with train_ratio=0.5 → 150 docs from the normal pool. So test = 150 docs (120 normal + 30 anomalous). This is the actual released protocol — great,

use it exactly.

Also random_state default = 42, and np.random.seed(42) then np.random.choice(normal_indices, size=150, replace=False). Note: np.random.seed affects the global legacy RNG

.

"""Load the released Grammar benchmark and apply the authors' split protocol.

Data source: authors' repo (TokenCore), data/grammar.npy -- produced by
tokens_labels/json_to_npy.py from data/grammar_correction_labeled.json
(Label Studio export of the Kaggle "Grammar Correction" dataset).

Structure of the .npy: object array holding a dict with keys
  'sentences' : list[str]   (300)
  'tokens'    : list[list[str]]  word-level tokens per document
  'labels'    : list[list[int]]  0/1 token label per document

Split protocol: `split_anomaly_data` is reconstructed from the authors' own
compiled bytecode (eval.cpython-310.pyc, source d:\\Github\\TokenCore\\eval.py,
line 405) which Demo.ipynb calls with the default arguments
(train_ratio=0.5, random_state=42).  Disassembly (state/eval_dis.txt):

    y = np.array(y)
    n_train = int(len(X) * train_ratio)
    normal_indices = np.where(y == 0)[0]
    np.random.seed(random_state)
    train_indices = np.random.choice(normal_indices, size=n_train, replace=False)
    test_indices = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X)), train_indices)
    X_train = [X[i] for i in train_indices];  y_train = y[train_indices]
    X_test  = [X[i] for i in test_indices];   y_test  = y[test_indices]
    z_train = [z[i] for i in train_indices];  z_test  = [z[i] for i in test_indices]
    return X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, z_train, z_test

Note: n_train = int(len(X)*0.5) is 50% of ALL documents (300 -> 150), all drawn
from the normal pool, so the test set keeps 120 normal + 30 anomalous documents.
"""

import os
import numpy as np

REPO_DIR = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))), 'repo')
DATA_DIR = os.path.join(REPO_DIR, 'data')


def load_grammar(data_dir=DATA_DIR):
    """Return (sentences, tokens, labels) lists exactly as the authors released them."""
    path = os.path.join(data_dir, 'grammar.npy')
    data = np.load(path, allow_pickle=True).item()
    sentences = list(data['sentences'])
    tokens = [list(t) for t in data['tokens']]
    labels = [[int(x) for x in l] for l in data['labels']]
    return sentences, tokens, labels


def doc_labels(token_labels):
    """Paper Definition 2 / R11: a document is anomalous iff it has >=1 anomalous token.

    Same expression as Demo.ipynb cell 0:
        sentence_labels = [1 if any(labels) else 0 for labels in labels]
    """
    return [1 if any(l) else 0 for l in token_labels]


def split_anomaly_data(X, y, z, train_ratio=0.5, random_state=42):
    """Authors' split (recovered from their compiled eval.py, see module docstring)."""
    y = np.array(y)
    n_train = int(len(X) * train_ratio)
    normal_indices = np.where(y == 0)[0]
    np.random.seed(random_state)
    train_indices = np.random.choice(normal_indices, size=n_train, replace=False)
    test_indices = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X)), train_indices)
    X_train = [X[i] for i in train_indices]
    y_train = y[train_indices]
    X_test = [X[i] for i in test_indices]
    y_test = y[test_indices]
    z_train = [z[i] for i in train_indices]
    z_test = [z[i] for i in test_indices]
    return X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, z_train, z_test


def check_grammar(sentences, tokens, labels, y_docs):
    """Intermediate checks from the plan (R10 / R11). Returns a report dict."""
    n_docs = len(sentences)
    n_anom_docs = int(sum(y_docs))
    n_norm_docs = n_docs - n_anom_docs
    n_tokens = sum(len(t) for t in tokens)
    n_pos_tokens = sum(sum(l) for l in labels)
    # R11: document label == any token label
    inconsistent = [i for i in range(n_docs) if y_docs[i] != (1 if any(labels[i]) else 0)]
    # normal documents must carry no anomalous token
    norm_with_pos = [i for i in range(n_docs) if y_docs[i] == 0 and any(labels[i])]
    anom_without_pos = [i for i in range(n_docs) if y_docs[i] == 1 and not any(labels[i])]
    assert len(sentences) == len(tokens) == len(labels)
    assert all(len(s) == len(l) for s, l in zip(tokens, labels)), 'token/label length mismatch'
    report = {
        'n_docs': n_docs,
        'n_normal_docs': n_norm_docs,
        'n_anomalous_docs': n_anom_docs,
        'doc_anomaly_rate': round(n_anom_docs / n_docs, 4),
        'n_tokens': n_tokens,
        'n_positive_tokens': n_pos_tokens,
        'token_positive_rate': round(n_pos_tokens / n_tokens, 5),
        'doc_token_label_inconsistencies': len(inconsistent),
        'normal_docs_with_positive_tokens': len(norm_with_pos),
        'anomalous_docs_without_positive_tokens': len(anom_without_pos),
    }
    return report

"""BERT-base-uncased word-embedding front-end.

The pooling logic is NOT re-implemented: we call the authors' own
`repo/align.py::extract_word_embeddings`, which (lines 109-147) does the
element-wise max over the subword vectors of each word (paper Eq. 1 / R2) and
skips special tokens (word_idx is None for [CLS]/[SEP]/[PAD]) -- A4.
It returns, per document, a list of dicts {'token','embedding','label',
'subword_position'}, i.e. exactly one unit per gold word token (R9).

`load_bert` resolves bert-base-uncased from the shared HF cache first
(REPRO_DATA_CACHE/hf/hub) so the clean re-run does not re-download.
"""

import contextlib
import io
import os
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))), 'repo'))

MODEL_NAME = 'bert-base-uncased'


def hf_cache_dir():
    cache = os.environ.get('REPRO_DATA_CACHE')
    if cache:
        p = os.path.join(cache, 'hf', 'hub')
        if os.path.isdir(p):
            return p
    return None


def load_bert(model_name=MODEL_NAME, device='cpu'):
    import torch
    from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel
    kwargs = {}
    cd = hf_cache_dir()
    if cd:
        kwargs['cache_dir'] = cd
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name, **kwargs)
    model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_name, **kwargs)
    model = model.to(device).eval()
    torch.set_num_threads(os.cpu_count() or 4)
    return model, tokenizer


def extract_word_embeddings(model, tokenizer, all_tokens, all_labels,
                            model_name=MODEL_NAME, device='cpu', log_path=None):
    """Call the authors' align.extract_word_embeddings, silencing its stdout.

    Returns the same structure: list (per document) of list of dicts with keys
    'token', 'embedding' (np.ndarray, 768,), 'label', 'subword_position'.
    """
    from align import extract_word_embeddings as _authors_extract

    buf = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
        result = _authors_extract(
            model=model,
            tokenizer=tokenizer,
            all_tokens=all_tokens,
            all_labels=all_labels,
            model_name=model_name,
            local_cache_dir=hf_cache_dir(),
            device=device,
        )
    if log_path:
        os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(log_path), exist_ok=True)
        with open(log_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
            f.write(buf.getvalue())
    return result


def flatten(sentences):
    """Demo.ipynb cell 2/3: X = np.array([item['embedding'] for sent in train_data for item in sent])"""
    import numpy as np
    X = np.array([item['embedding'] for sent in sentences for item in sent])
    z = [item['label'] for sent in sentences for item in sent]
    lengths = [len(sent) for sent in sentences]
    return X, z, lengths

def fit_scores(X_train, X_test):

"""Reproduce claim C1 (and C2 + document-level by-products) of
"Towards Token-Level Text Anomaly Detection" (arXiv 2601.13644):
TokenCore token-level AUROC / AUPRC on the Grammar benchmark.

Pipeline (identical to the authors' Demo.ipynb, only the missing driver is rebuilt):
  1. load the released Grammar benchmark (repo/data/grammar.npy: 300 docs,
     270 normal + 30 anomalous, 10% anomaly rate -- R10)
  2. split with the authors' eval.split_anomaly_data (recovered from their
     compiled bytecode): 50% of the documents, drawn from the normal pool only,
     become the memory-bank training set; the rest (normal + all anomalous) is
     the test set (R6)
  3. word-level embeddings = element-wise max pooling of BERT subword embeddings
     (Eq. 1, R2) via the authors' unmodified repo/align.py, special tokens dropped (R9)
  4. memory bank = every word embedding of the normal training documents (R3),
     token score = distance to its nearest neighbour in the bank (Eq. 2, R4)
     via the authors' unmodified repo/TokenCore.py
  5. metrics: pooled token-level AUROC / AUPRC (R7) + document-level scores by
     mean aggregation of the token scores (Eq. 3, R5; the released eval.py uses
     max, both are reported).

Backbone arms: the released code (Demo.ipynb cell 1, align_batch.pyc default)
uses bert-base-cased, while Sec. 6.1 / R1 of the paper says BERT-base-uncased.
We run the authors' cased backbone as the PRIMARY arm and uncased as a
cross-check arm, and report both.

Usage:
  python reproduce.py                 # both arms, seed 42 (authors' default)
  python reproduce.py --smoke         # 10 documents, end-to-end plumbing check
  python reproduce.py --search        # split-seed sensitivity sweep (not in the default run)
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
import time

import numpy as np

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(HERE, 'src'))

import data_grammar as dg          # noqa: E402
import embed_bert as eb            # noqa: E402
import detector as det             # noqa: E402
import evaluate as ev              # noqa: E402

RESULTS_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, 'results')
LOG_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, 'logs')

PRIMARY_MODEL = 'bert-base-cased'      # as used by the authors' released code
CROSSCHECK_MODEL = 'bert-base-uncased'  # as stated in Sec. 6.1 / R1
DEFAULT_SEED = 42                      # authors' split_anomaly_data default


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# embedding cache: per-document word embeddings, independent of the split
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def embed_documents(model, tokenizer, tokens, labels, model_name, tag, device='cpu'):
    t0 = time.time()
    data = eb.extract_word_embeddings(model, tokenizer, tokens, labels,
                                      model_name=model_name, device=device,
                                      log_path=os.path.join(LOG_DIR, f'align_{tag}.log'))
    assert len(data) == len(tokens)
    per_doc = []
    for i, sent in enumerate(data):
        X = np.array([item['embedding'] for item in sent])
        z = [int(item['label']) for item in sent]
        assert X.shape[0] == len(tokens[i]), (
            f'alignment failure in doc {i}: {X.shape[0]} units vs {len(tokens[i])} gold tokens')
        assert X.shape[1] == 768, f'embedding width {X.shape[1]} != 768'
        assert all((a is None) == (b is None) for a, b in zip(z, labels[i])), f'label drift doc {i}'
        per_doc.append({'index': i, 'n_units': X.shape[0], 'X': X, 'z': z})
    print(f'  embedded {len(per_doc)} docs in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s '
          f'({sum(d["n_units"] for d in per_doc)} word units)')
    return per_doc


def assemble(per_doc, indices):
    X = np.concatenate([per_doc[i]['X'] for i in indices], axis=0)
    z = [v for i in indices for v in per_doc[i]['z']]
    lengths = [per_doc[i]['n_units'] for i in indices]
    return X, z, lengths


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def run_arm(per_doc, doc_label, tokens, train_pos, test_pos, model_name, seed):
    """Memory bank on the train tokens, score the test tokens, compute metrics."""
    X_train, z_train, _ = assemble(per_doc, train_pos)
    X_test, z_test, lengths_test = assemble(per_doc, test_pos)
    y_test = [int(doc_label[i]) for i in test_pos]

    clf = det.build_tokencore()
    clf.fit(X_train)                       # R3: full bank of normal-training tokens
    scores = clf.decision_function(X_test)  # R4: nearest-neighbour distance

    tm = ev.token_metrics(z_test, scores)
    doc_mean = ev.document_scores(scores, lengths_test, 'mean')   # Eq. 3 / R5
    doc_max = ev.document_scores(scores, lengths_test, 'max')     # authors' released eval.py
    dm_mean = ev.document_metrics(y_test, doc_mean)
    dm_max = ev.document_metrics(y_test, doc_max)

    # sanity: training tokens scored against their own bank give near-zero distances
    d_train = clf.decision_function(X_train)
    return {
        'model': model_name,
        'seed': seed,
        'n_train_docs': int(len(train_pos)),
        'n_test_docs': int(len(test_pos)),
        'n_bank_tokens': int(X_train.shape[0]),
        'n_test_tokens': int(X_test.shape[0]),
        'max_self_distance_on_train': float(d_train.max()),
        'token_level': tm,
        'doc_level_mean': dm_mean,
        'doc_level_max': dm_max,
    }

reason: within tolerance (|diff| 0.00468 <= 0.02) on a clean re-run

target.statement: TokenCore token-level AUROC on the Grammar dataset
target.table_ref: Table 1, Token section, row TokenCore, column Grammar ROC

tolerance.why: Rule 3: AUROC is a bounded score and the paper prints it in [0,1] as a fraction; no std/CI over repeated runs is reported (rule 1 inapplicable), and the token-level test set for Grammar is only ~150 documents' tokens, whose size is never stated as 2,000+ examples, so the smaller-set band of 0.02 absolute is used rather than the 0.01 of rule 2.

audit_summary: The reproduction implements the paper's core TokenCore pipeline faithfully: it uses the authors' unfixed repo code for max-pooling subword aggregation (Eq. 1), builds a memory bank from normal-training tokens only, scores test tokens by 1-NN Euclidean distance (Eq. 2), and computes pooled token-level AUROC/AUPRC plus document-level mean aggregation (Eq. 3). The target claim C1 (Grammar token AUROC, paper 0.6371 +/-0.02) is computed, not hardcoded: reproduce.py only contains 0.6371 in the comparison/pass logic, and the reported 0.6324 is a live roc_auc_score on 1419 test tokens (47 positive), passing with |diff|=0.0047. The main caveat is the backbone: the paper text says BERT-base-uncased, but the implementer ran bert-base-cased as the primary arm (with uncased as a cross-check giving 0.6137, which would actually fall just outside the +/-0.02 band). This choice is well-evidenced by the authors' released Demo.ipynb/align defaults and their compiled eval.pyc, and is fully disclosed in the code notes and assumption A13, but it is an inference rather than the paper's literal statement. R8 (the six baselines) is not implemented -- acceptable for this target but incomplete for the paper's full claim set -- and no scale-down occurred since the full 300-document benchmark and full memory bank were used. No anti-cheat flags apply: the number is computed on the correct data with the correct split family and metric.

requirement_check.evidence: The run embeds with BERT (max-pooled word embeddings) but the PRIMARY arm uses bert-base-cased, not bert-base-uncased as R1/Sec.6.1 states; bert-base-uncased is only reported as a cross-check arm. Justification (A13) is strong: Demo.ipynb cell 1 and align_batch/align defaults use bert-base-cased, and the cased arm reproduces the paper's document PRC 0.2624 to four decimals. Both arms are reported in metrics.json, but the headline C1 value comes from cased.

Element-wise max pooling over subwords is used via the authors' repo/align.py and independently verified in reproduce.py::_check_maxpool (log: '[check] element-wise max pooling verified on doc 10 (6 words, 2 subwords max)').
Memory bank is built only from normal-training token embeddings; run_arm asserts int(np.asarray(z_train).sum())==0 and n_bank_tokens=1327 for the 150 normal training docs.
Token score = nearest-neighbor (Euclidean, k=1) distance via the authors' TokenCore.decision_function; train-token self-distance max = 6.7e-7, confirming a genuine NN lookup rather than a proxy.

Document scores are computed by mean aggregation of token scores per Eq. (3) (doc_level_mean reported), with the authors' max aggregation also reported for transparency. Not relevant to the token-level target C1 but correctly implemented.

Split uses 50% (=150) of documents drawn from the normal pool for training, remaining 150 (120 normal + 30 anomalous) for test, via the recovered authors' split_anomaly_data(random_state=42); consistent with Demo.ipynb and the paper's protocol.
Both AUROC and AUPRC are computed at token and document level (token_auroc, token_auprc_authors/sklearn, doc_auroc, doc_auprc_authors/sklearn).

None of the six baselines (LOF, iForest, ECOD, DeepSVDD, AutoEncoder, LUNAR) were implemented; only TokenCore is run. The match target C1 is TokenCore's own value, so this does not affect the target, but the comparison set required by R8 is absent.
Subword embeddings are aggregated to one unit per gold word; reproduce.py asserts X.shape[0]==len(tokens[i]) and 768-dim width for every document (no alignment failures).
Data checks confirm n_docs=300, normal=270, anomalous=30, anomaly rate 0.10, loaded from the authors' released repo/data/grammar.npy.
Document labels derived as '1 if any(token label)' giving 0 doc/token inconsistencies, 0 normal docs with positive tokens, 0 anomalous docs without positive tokens.
